The text broadly defines three main topics that dominate the European strategic landscape—domestic coherence and international relevance, the existence of an unstable neighborhood, and economic prosperity. There are many papers, books, and other materials dealing with the prospects of European geostrategy and geopolitics. To name one example,

European Geostrategy presented four priorities that are crucial for the European security—stabilizing its neighborhood, contributing to maritime security, contributing to the UN collective security, and contributing to internal security
(Biscop et al. 2016). These priorities are coherent with the selected three fields as are other more detailed works.1

Even though the works predicting the future institutional setting of the European project in accordance with the nature of European political realities differ widely—from promoting solutions from the close and strong union (Simms 2012) to the development of the set of overlapping and decentralized agencies (Zielonka 2014)—it is clear that the return to the sovereign nation-state system as took place throughout the nineteenth century would move the European international relevance firmly into the shadows of more important players like the PRC or the United States.

Finally, the vital part of the common European project is the economic and social development of the continent. From the economic point of view, we must highlight two issues—the freedom of trade and access to energy sources. The first issue is mainly connected, as noted earlier by the European Geostrategy priorities, to the issue of maritime trade that is key for the European development. The freedom of navigation across the Atlantic or the sea routes to China and the safety of ships are keys to the economic prosperity of Europe in the long term.
Given the energy situation, the EU tries to secure the sources of energies by forcing its energy policies abroad
and disrupting the Russian hegemony by market tools aimed at weakening its position

(Kuzemko and Hadfield 2016, p. 34), diversification (Kuzemko and Hadfield 2016, p. 35), the change of its energy production capabilities that is also connected to the issue of climate change mitigation (Verda 2016, p. 72), and to a certain degree keeping Russia in mutual dependency status that does not allow the long-term disruptions of primarily natural gas imports (Godzimirski 2016b, p. 91). Also in 2014, the EU launched its Energy Union that should secure the energy needs of the continent for the time to come (Godzimirski 2016b, p. 105). The European energy market, nevertheless, still faces many challenges. According to Z. Daojiang (2016, p. 116), the three most relevant ones are the decrease in the EU primary energy production, dynamic changes in the energy mix with uncertain demand, and growing dependency. What the solution for these issues is remains to be seen; the most logical way would be the diversification of the places of origin for these resources that would include imports from the United States. The country is currently coming through a shale revolution that will probably turn it into an energy exporter. This relationship holds, however, many obstacles (Conley et al. 2016). The second solution is the proliferation of new means of energy generation and savings that will follow the anticipated green revolution in energy production.

The pursuit of the European strategic goals has some limitations regarding the means applied by the union. These are connected to the focus on the utilization of the soft power and pull factors—to make countries want to be on good terms with economically and normatively strong Europe.5 The strategy has not only become an outcome of the historical and normative development on the continent since the end of the Second World War but is also a reflection of the lack of hard power capabilities. In a situation where national armies of selected armies possess some useful military forces (e.g., the United Kingdom or France), the common security framework is still highly dependent on the provision of the US umbrella via theNATO framework. This turns Europe into the center of cooperation rather than conflict but also limits its options in case the partnership does not work out. As evident from the conflicts in former Yugoslavia or Libya, Europe is unable to make use of the limited hard power potential it holds. Furthermore, as apparent from the case of post-Ukrainian conflict sanctions aimed at the Russian economy, its available nonmilitary options are also of limited use.6 The point here is not to evaluate the strengths and weaknesses as well as the success of this approach. The ESA on its key 2014 Ministerial Meeting adopted three resolutions aimed at the continuation of the development of technologies, providing Europeans with access to outer space. These resolutions include the setting up of Ariane 6 and the Vega C programs, the establishment of the ESA’s three destinations of exploration—LEO, Moon, and Mars—and the creation of a vision for the ESA development until 2030 (ESA 2014c). The primary objectives for space development are broadly set as space exploration, economics, global cooperation, and inspiration for future generations (ESA 2014d, p. 7).7 As evident, the stated strategic goals fit into the three strategic priorities noted in the previous section—a common approach and an influential role of the EU in international politics, security, and economics. This position was further strengthened by the passing of the US export restrictions in 1998 that cut many US industries off international projects (Johnson-Freese 2007, pp. 161–163). The common European space activities, despite being demonstratively non-offensive, do not omit the military dimension (Mutschler and Venet 2012, p. 118). Notwithstanding the issues connected to the development of the common European strategy and coordination among the EU and ESA members (de Montluc 2012; Mutschler and Venet 2012, pp. 120–121), the organizations understand the strategic importance of establishing a critical space infrastructure. This infrastructure can be realistically created only in a common framework (Al-Rodhan 2012, pp. 120–121; Petroni et al. 2009, pp. 53–54). The main projects that relate to the issue of the common position of European countries and to the issue of security are Galileo, Copernicus, and the push for an establishment of a more independent and capable Space Situational Awareness Programme (Al-Rodhan 2012, p. 123; Giannopapa 2012, p. 270).
